title: The art of the tariff pause can trump all this chaos around trade deal
text:
Warren Buffett said that tariffs are an act of war.  Hopefully, the world is beyond a hot military war between the two largest economic and nuclear-armed military forces on the planet. There is a genuine competition for supremacy between the US and China, which has evolved over the past 2 decades, after Nixon’s famous “Shanghai Communique” in 1972 that led to a thaw in relations and greater cooperation. 

The subsequent rise of Chinese manufacturing (now 30% of the world’s output) saw a great uplift for the Chinese population from abject poverty, but perhaps at the expense of hollowing out of jobs in the US.  China has moved up the value chain from making underwear to chips, electric cars, automation, AI, and having large stores of rare earth minerals. The knock against China as stealing and copying everything from the West is probably less true at this stage.  What about the moral outrage that China is "ripping us off"? Is that justified and accurate with reality on the ground, in terms of relative cost of living, quality of life of an average individual? Well, that depends on your personal value system and perspective!

Karl Rove (Republican strategist) wrote the following:  "Contrary to today’s populist doomsayers, this truism has served America well because our people are so good at inventing and making things. The per-capita GDP of the U.S. in current dollars grew from $36,330 in 2000 to $82,769 in 2023, the last year for which global numbers are available. That’s a $46,439 increase for every American.

By comparison, global per-capita GDP in current dollars rose $7,675 over that same period. China only grew $11,655. If our country is being ripped off by the rest of the world because U.S. companies depend on “cheap labor,” as the vice president claims, you wouldn’t expect America’s per-capita GDP increase to be six times that of the world as a whole." https://www.wsj.com/opinion/the-art-of-the-tariff-pause-can-trump-all-this-chaos-around-trade-deal-6de40f42?mod=hp_opin_pos_5#cxrecs_s

The growth of China has unnerved its neighbors as well as both parties in the US.  This is perceived as existential national security threat.  The current showdown of conflict is manifesting most visibly as tariffs but is part of a larger trade war which may involve a variety of tools and weapons, meant to harm the enemy.

Trade wars between the United States and China involve a range of economic tools designed to exert pressure, protect domestic interests, or retaliate against perceived unfair practices. These tools go beyond simple tariffs, encompassing a mix of policy levers that can disrupt markets, shift supply chains, and influence global trade dynamics. Below, I’ll discuss the key tools employed by both nations, drawing on their recent history—particularly the escalation since 2018 and the latest developments as of April 9, 2025.

Tools Used by the United States

1. Tariffs 

o Description: Taxes on imported goods to raise their cost, making domestic products more competitive.
o Examples: The U.S. kicked off the trade war in 2018 under Trump with 25% tariffs on $50 billions of Chinese goods (Section 301), targeting tech and industrial items. By 2019, this ballooned to $550 billion in imports. In 2025, Trump’s “Liberation Day” (April 2) introduced a 20% tariff on nearly all imports, with threats of 50% more on Chinese goods, pushing rates above 100% in some cases.
o Impact: Raises costs for U.S. consumers (e.g., 10â30% price hikes on intermediate goods, per the Peterson Institute) and pressures China’s export-driven economy, though it also sparked $30 billion in farmer subsidies (2018â2020).

2. Export Controls 

o Description: Restrictions on selling sensitive technologies or materials to China.
o Examples: The U.S. Commerce Department’s Entity List has blacklisted firms like Huawei since 2019, barring them from U.S. tech (e.g., semiconductors). In 2024, controls tightened on AI chips and manufacturing tools, aiming to curb China’s military and tech advances.
o Impact: Slows China’s innovation—Huawei’s 5G rollout stumbled—but risks U.S. firms losing market share as China seeks alternatives.

3. Investment Restrictions 

o Description: Limits on Chinese investment in U.S. companies or sectors.
o Examples: The Committee on Foreign Investment in the U.S. (CFIUS) blocked deals like Ant Financials’ 2018 bid for MoneyGram. Post-2025, scrutiny intensified on Chinese stakes in tech and critical infrastructure.
o Impact: Protects national security but shrinks capital flows, potentially stunting U.S. startups reliant on foreign cash.

4. Sanctions and Blacklists 

o Description: Targeting specific entities with financial or trade penalties.
o Examples: In 2025, the U.S. added 11 Chinese firms to its “unreliable entity” list for alleged Taiwan military ties, freezing their U.S. dealings.
o Impact: Isolates key players, though enforcement gaps and global workarounds dilute the sting.

5. Subsidies and Domestic Support 

o Description: Boosting U.S. industries to counter China’s edge.
o Examples: The 2022 CHIPS Act ($52 billion) pumps money into domestic semiconductor production, while 2025 budget talks eye more manufacturing incentives.
o Impact: Builds resilience but strains federal coffers—tariffs alone raised $258 billion in 2025, per the Tax Foundation.

Tools Used by China

1. Retaliatory Tariffs 

o Description: Mirror taxes on U.S. imports to hit American exporters.
o Examples: In 2018, China slapped 25% tariffs on $16 billion of U.S. goods (soybeans, cars). In April 2025, it countered Trump’s latest wave with 34% tariffs on all U.S. imports—soybeans, cotton, and more—escalating from earlier targeted levies.
o Impact: Slashes U.S. agricultural exports ($27 billion lost, 2018â2019, USDA) and stokes domestic support for Xi Jinping, though it raises China’s import costs.

2. Export Restrictions 

o Description: Limiting access to critical materials China dominates.
o Examples: In 2025, China curbed exports of rare earths (e.g., samarium, dysprosium) and minerals like tungsten—vital for U.S. tech and defense—after Trump’s February tariffs tied to the fentanyl crisis.
o Impact: Threatens U.S. supply chains (China supplies 80% of rare earths), but risks alienating other trade partners if overplayed.

3. Currency Manipulation 

o Description: Adjusting the yuan to offset tariff pain or boost exports.
o Examples: In 2019, the yuan hit 7-to-1 against the dollar, prompting a U.S. “manipulator” label. In 2025, posts on X suggest China’s tweaking it again to counter Trump’s 65% effective tariff rate.
o Impact: Cheapens Chinese goods abroad but risks inflation at home and global backlash.

4. Anti-Sanctions Laws and Blacklists 

o Description: Legal tools to punish foreign firms complying with U.S. measures.
o Examples: China’s 2021 Anti-Foreign Sanctions Law was beefed up in 2025, targeting U.S. companies like FedEx for tariff compliance. Its “unreliable entity” list now mirrors U.S. blacklists.
o Impact: Deters multinationals from siding with the U.S., though enforcement remains spotty.

5. Market Access Restrictions 

o Description: Limiting U.S. firms’ operations in China.
o Examples: In 2024, tightened rules hit Apple and Tesla—subtle barriers like slower approvals—while 2025 saw U.S. farm import qualifications suspended.
o Impact: Squeezes U.S. profits (China’s a $462 billion market for U.S. goods, 2024 BEA data) but could backfire if foreign investment flees.

Comparative Analysis

â¢ Leverage: The U.S. wields more tariff power due to China’s $295 billion trade surplus (2024), giving Trump’s “65% rate” bite—China’s exporters can’t survive without U.S. markets, per Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent. China’s rare earth chokehold, though, gives it a strategic edge the U.S. can’t match short-term.
â¢ Efficiency: Tariffs are blunt—U.S. consumers bore 90% of 2018â2019 costs (Fajgelbaum study)—while China’s export curbs are precise but limited by its own reliance on global trade (e.g., EU imports outpace U.S.).
â¢ Escalation: Both escalate fast—U.S. tariffs jumped from 20% to 54% pre-2025, then threatened 115%; China’s 34% blanket tariff hit April 10, 2025. Export controls and blacklists signal a shift to tech and resource wars, per Evan Medeiros’ “new arsenal” comment.

Broader Implications

These tools don’t just slug it out—they reshape trade. Bystander nations (Mexico, Vietnam) gained $450 billion in exports from 2018â2019 shifts (Yale study), while U.S.-China decoupling risks a global recession—crude oil slumped 7% in April 2025 (Politico). China pivots to domestic demand and allies (e.g., India talks), but its overcapacity—flooding markets with cheap goods—keeps the fight alive. The U.S., betting on tariffs and tech dominance, could overplay its hand if allies balk at collateral damage.

In short, this trade war’s toolbox—tariffs, bans, subsidies, and more—is a high-stakes game of economic chicken. Neither side’s winning clean; both are bleeding, and the world’s picking up the tab.

text:
I have expressed deep skepticism and worry at the direction public health is going in our country.  It is being politicized by long-standing "ideology" by special interest groups with fringe ideas, despite alarm from those with content expertise, long-standing medical practice, and published data. This is not confined to Trump and his cabinet (including RFK), but also by local groups at state levels. There is a cabal of anti-science.  

Examples include the move to pass legislation to make fringe therapies such as ivermectin (an approved anti-helminthic drug) for OTC use for covid, or removal of fluoride from public water supplies, or a wink-wink nod against routine vaccinations (i.e. MMR in west Texas).  I worry that additional approaches will take root in the name of "alternative medicine" (supplements, nutrition, etc.).  Public health being politicized will disproportionately affect areas of the country and people most vulnerable.  We need to be critical about the motivations (and conflicts of interest) of the peddlers as opposed to the public interest.  

It is great to have an "open mind" in science and research and allow "out of the box" thinking. However, with limited resources, scientists cannot afford to chase down every possible idea and have to be strategic about which approaches have an optimal cost-benefit.  Who decides that and how does that work? Obviously, content expertise is critical and adherence to sound principles of science, which does have built--in questioning and reproducibility as part of the methodology.

Perhaps we need to hit a bottom, both vividly and publicly, in healthcare and the economy, before we reestablish trust in expertise.

title: Say hello to your new colleague the ai agent productivity boost workplace
text:
There is much hype about AI. I have fully embraced various LLMs for both research and first drafts.  That has been wonderous but still small potatoes. We are increasingly hearing about "AI agents" where language can be converted into "action", whether for businesses (replacing painful phone menus, etc.) or for consumers (booking a trip, etc.).  And about using our devices (smart phone/watches, smart speakers, cars, cameras) as a verbal hands-free interface to make simple things happen.  As imagination meets technology and profit motive, these incremental changes will revolutionize much of what we do in our daily lives. People that could adapt to these changes (rather than throw up their hands) will do better, personally as well as professionally!  This is near-term future (i.e. 2-4 years).

This editorial by Marc Benioff (CEO of Salesforce) is self-serving to promote his Agent, but this is being pursued by all the players in every industry.  What a time to be alive?

title: Trump tariffs china
text:
I am not an alarmist or fanboy of Chinese greatness. This editorial by Friedman in NYT Op-Ed gives a glimpse of the current dynamic.  I think the US is fighting the last war, with a push to bring most manufacturing onshore. At the same time, we are not addressing serious workforce training needs for the future and assaulting expertise/education at all levels.  Finally, we are stuck in divisive culture wars that are not “winnable.”
 
Friedman posits “the only win-win deal is one that I’d call: Made in America, by American workers, in partnership with Chinese technology, capital and experts. That is, we just reverse the strategy China used to get wealthy in the 1990s, which was: Made in China, by Chinese workers, with American, European, Korean and Japanese technology, capital and partners.”

 “Interdependence is no longer our choice. It’s our condition. Our only choice is whether we forge healthy interdependencies, and rise together, or maintain unhealthy interdependence and fall together.”

In a showdown with China that we are clearly entering:  China does NOT have midterm elections!  Which means that in a capricious political war, they will likely have time on their side c/w democratic nations!

There is additional alarm about the advances being made by the Chinese in biomedical research:

text:
I have been quite vocal at the slash and burn approach that DOGE has taken to government agencies in general, and research funding, universities, public health, and NIH in particular.  

Having said that, those with inside knowledge of the process also need to step up and voice constructive ways to improve the process. This is part of the concept of "institutional renewal" that is critical for a bureaucracy and government to stay relevant and responsive to the times.  Not only at the NIH but all other agencies. Before I get hateful comments, let me be clear, I am not in favor of the current approach at change!

The National Institutes of Health (NIH) is the backbone of U.S. biomedical research, funneling roughly $45 billion annually into grants that shape science and medicine. It’s a behemoth meant to drive breakthroughs—think penicillin or mRNA vaccines—but the current funding and grant review system is a creaking machine, riddled with inefficiencies, biases, and misaligned incentives. Are we getting what we pay for? Not even close. Here’s why.

First, the grant review process is a meat grinder of conservatism. Peer review panels, stacked with established scientists, favor safe, incremental proposals over bold, high-risk ideas. A 2015 study in Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences found that innovative projects—those with novel keywords or unconventional approaches—score lower, as reviewers cling to familiarity. The result? We fund what’s already worked, not what could transform. Take the Human Genome Project: initially dismissed as pie-in-the-sky, it barely scraped by on non-NIH cash before proving its worth. Today’s system would’ve strangled it in the crib.

Second, the hyper-competitive funding climate—only 19% of R01 grants were funded in 2023—turns scientists into grant-writing drones. Researchers spend up to 40% of their time chasing money, per a 2016 Nature survey, not doing science. This churn burns out talent and skews priorities toward trendy buzzwords like “AI” or “precision medicine,” even if the science is shaky. Look at Alzheimer’s research: decades of NIH billions dumped into amyloid-beta hypotheses yielded little beyond failed drugs, while alternative theories starved. We’re paying for proposals that sound good, not results that deliver.

Third, the system’s bloated with inequity. A 2021 NIH analysis showed Black applicants are 10% less likely to get funded than white peers, even controlling for credentials. Meanwhile, a handful of elite institutions—think Harvard, Stanford—hoover up 20% of the pot, per 2022 data, leaving mid-tier labs scrabbling. This isn’t meritocracy; it’s a club. And don’t get started on the “Matthew effect”: big names with prior grants keep winning, while young investigators, who often bring fresh ideas, get crumbs—only 2% of NIH funds go to those under 36.

Are we getting cures, insights, value? Sometimes, sure—NIH-backed work on CAR-T therapy or HIV antiretrovirals proves it can shine. But too often, we’re bankrolling a self-perpetuating cycle: safe science, padded CVs, and papers that pile up in journals nobody reads. A 2023 PLOS ONE study estimated 30% of NIH-funded trials fail to publish results within five years. That’s taxpayer money vanishing into a black hole.

The fix? Slash the bureaucracy—cut redundant compliance hoops that eat 20% of grant budgets, per a 2018 National Academies report. Cap institutional overhead (some universities skim 50%+). And overhaul reviews: blind them to applicant identity, prioritize risk over polish, and reward outcomes, not promises. Until then, we’re not buying breakthroughs—we’re subsidizing a status quo that’s more about survival than science.

A humorous discussion of the ills of our current grant funding process was satirized in Genome Biology in 2012 by Gregory Petsko. He used the example of Christopher Columbus asking for funding assistance from King Ferdinand of Spain to cross the Atlantic without first having "preliminary data", being too risky, etc.!

https://genomebiology.biomedcentral.com/counter/pdf/10.1186/gb-2012-13-5-155.pdf

I look forward to thoughtful comments and opportunities for improvement.

title: Trump trade war game
text:
A zero-sum mindset in negotiations assumes that resources are limited, and one party's gain is another's loss—like splitting a fixed pie. It often leads to competitive, rigid strategies where trust is low, and the focus is on claiming the biggest share, sometimes at the expense of long-term relationships.

A win-win approach, by contrast, sees negotiations as an opportunity to create value for both sides. It’s about expanding the pie before dividing it, through collaboration, open communication, and finding mutual benefits. Think of it as two chefs working together to bake a bigger cake, rather than fighting over crumbs.

The zero-sum view can work in one-off deals with no future stakes, but win-win tends to build stronger, lasting outcomes—especially when trust and creativity are on the table.   

Since WW2, the US has led a rule based playing field with multi-lateral trade, where everyone profited (including the US). We should ask the question why did manufacturers move overseas? Market forces dictate that the living standards, cost of living AND wages are much higher in the US, and it was more "efficient" for the marketplace to cut labor costs.  The upside of that has been lower cost of goods for the average consumer, but the downside has involved displacement of workers in select sectors. So, what is the net- net?  If you pursue a strategy that forces manufacturing back into the US, there will be an inevitable increased cost of goods and less efficiency.  How does this play out with the backdrop of increase in robotics and AI? I would argue that is a much bigger threat to manufacturing jobs than going overseas (imho).

The current strategy of tariffs upends that into individual trade deals with each country with separate rules, which leads to chaos, is arbitrary based on the whims of a mercurial leader, and sows distrust and the potential for newer alliances that may not be beneficial to us.  The simulation noted in this study is highly theoretical and assumes a purely rational decision-making, however we know we are dealing with human beings!

This op-ed by Jamal Bouie NYT captures this instinct to dominate in a zero-sum mindset!

title: Pro Tip, my friends!
text:
Pro Tip, my friends!  We all get various outrage videos sent to us (or we come across them), some are silly and humorous, but others are serious, and you might wonder about the veracity of content, etc.  Most have been forwarded multiple times and there is no label or a reference or attribution. So, what to do?  Beyond simply rolling my eyes and/or seething with madness, I found a solution. Simply copy the you tube link and paste it into your favorite AI engine, such as GROK (my recent go to or chatGPT), and walla!  

As an example, check this video out.  I thought it was insanely negative and biased so I wanted to know who produced it and what might be their motive.  GROK provided a quick starting point to chase down their agenda, etc.  Of course, you still have to do due diligence as to accuracy, etc. I thought this was a great example, based on initial response from GROK, I further researched the Wilks Brothers, Texas billionaires from the shale and oil industry with an ultra-conservative Christian nationalism worldview.  Helpful from a research standpoint so you can further make-up your mind!

YouTube Short at https://youtube.com/shorts/IcK4wVtAErU?si=BhgT5ZgeyKCIRzxC was produced by PragerU (via its PragerU Shorts channel) and funded through PragerU’s donor-supported budget, likely including contributions from major conservative donors like the Wilks brothers and its broader supporter network. No specific external funding entity is confirmed for this particular video beyond PragerU’s typical financial structure.

In our professional worlds, we have certain tools at our disposal to at least attempt to validate sources. But we all need a framework for other areas, so we do not get sucked into a vortex of misinformation!

title: This is an interesting perspective of how we adapt.
text:
This is an interesting perspective of how we adapt.
The article "The Curious Personality Changes of Older Age" by Faith Hill explores how personality can evolve in older age, particularly when individuals face a loss of control over their circumstances. As people age, they often encounter situations such as declining health, reduced independence, or shifting social roles that limit their ability to shape their environment. In response, some undergo notable personality shifts. These changes are not merely reactions to external pressures but can reflect an adaptive process, where the self evolves to cope with new realities. Hill suggests that such transformations challenge the common assumption that personality remains static in adulthood, highlighting the resilience and complexity of human identity in later life.  In fact, adaptations to navigate the world requires new learning and resilience! All good things!

title: On my FB page, I really am striving not to get sucked into the outrage of partisan
text:
On my FB page, I really am striving not to get sucked into the outrage of partisan politics and reacting to every outrage, tweet, etc. We all have world views and biases, but the goal of reading and research is to have an open mind and to try to make sense of unfolding events.  There is clearly deep dissatisfaction in the US and a desire for change and policy differences. Beyond personalities, we need to separate signals from noise. Even though Trump and Musk are highly visible personalities, I am trying to make a coherent sense for the intellectual context and world view of their policies.  

This episode of Ezra Klein, with Gillian Tett, an economist at Financial Times (and anthropologist historian) has helped me. 

There is clearly a global reset going on as part of “Make America Great Again”, affecting trade, economic, tech, and military sectors. The goal is to move from our current “neo-liberal order” (where free trade is king) to a “mercantilist or hegemonic power structure,” where the strategy is to use global financial and trading systems and any tactics to leverage power and achieve your objective.  

This leads to an emerging “Mara-a-Lago Accord.”  American power in the world today is NOT manufacturing (where China dominates), but a dollar-based financial system, where the American Federal Reserve and Treasury dominate. There are some global rumblings to displace the dollar, with alternative systems (Euro, Yuan, etc.).  So, the strategic goal is to keep the dollar as dominant. However, there is also a sense that the dollar is “overvalued” as evidenced by the large trade deficits or imbalances with many countries, which makes goods cheap for the US consumer, but it undermines US manufacturing and hollows out jobs. So, their vision is to try to reconcile the fact they want to keep the dollar dominant, but they also want to weaken its value, which is the so-called Mar-a-Lago Accord. It would essentially entail a number of countries coming together to agree to weaken the dollar and, in exchange, America offering some form of tariff relief, some form of military protection, being allies and potentially doing other things like maybe swapping long-term U.S. debt for other forms of debt.

Large US debt ($36T) is a problem (US GDP is $28T so debt is 125% GDP) where the annual interest payments are substantial and rising (larger than defense budget of about $1T). There are finite ways to resolve this: 1. Just go into default (last resort), 2. Cut expenses, especially defense (as Bannon advocates) or entitlement programs such as social security or Medicaid or Medicare (all highly contentious); 3. Grow our way out by stimulating the economy (our GDP is about 2%, far-fetched to grow this to what is required); 4. Restructure the debt, by forcing allies to swap holdings of US Treasuries, $$, gold for “perpetual bonds” which will lower the debt or take it off the books (requires forcing other countries to accept). Other countries may need to be forced to do this financial engineering in exchange for “our military protection” or lower tariffs, etc. 

Scott Bessent is the Treasury Secretary, Stephen Miran is the Chair of Trump’s Council of Economic Affairs and Howard Lutnick is the Commerce Secretary who are the authors of the so called “Mara-Lago Accord.”

The current dynamic has been brewing for decades without acceptable solutions. The MAGA movement is proposing an approach, though aggressive, to tackle these issues and the outcome remains to be seen as to how the rest of the world (and domestic audience) will react. 

New terms for me:  "sane-washing" = reporting on Trump that makes things sound saner than they really are; “theory-washing” = take things that are gestural, instinctual, contradictory and make a theory out of it. 

These episodes are intense, deep, and do have a high "nerd factor," but feel free to comment on this."

title: Tariffs:  Tools to impact economic policy and US economy (i.e.
text:
Tariffs:  Tools to impact economic policy and US economy (i.e. bring back manufacturing and jobs) or is it a tool for corruption / consolidation of power / patronage of the favored?

Tariff is a consumption tax and is regressive in that it disproportionately affects the lower 80% of the income distribution, since consumption is a bigger portion of their income. Most serious economic studies dating from McKinley to Smoot-Hawley to recent era (including the Trump 1.0) indicates that Tariffs do not contribute to improving the US economy.  

Tariff is a tool that is the purview of the executive branch, and it bypasses the Congress. It can be a power play, an act of war (as per Warren Buffett), and can be bypassed with carve outs at the whims of the President.

In Trump 2.0, the combination of tariffs and extension of the massive tax cuts is a strategy of bait-and-switch and obfuscation of the general public. The populist base of lower income voters will be the group hurt most by these policies as discussed. This is the irony that needs to be understood.

This Ezra Klein episode is excellent, and the guest is Kimberly Clausing, a senior fellow at the Peterson Institute for International Economics.

text: This is a shoutout to “The Pitt”, a medical drama on HBO Max, set in a Pittsburgh ER. Each episode (1 hour shift) is entirely focused in the ER featuring a believable attending with a team of residents and medical students and nurses. This is the most realistic and accurate medical series that I have seen. The patient scenarios are common, the teaching points are typical, and the physicality of prep and equipment is on point.  Dr Robby’s approach to complex scenarios such as brain death, respiratory failure, teen pregnancy etc is authentic. The content is largely focused with limited interpersonal drama.  I suspect this will appeal to healthcare workers as to relevance and accuracy and to lay public for the visceral realism. I found myself going through the differential diagnosis, etc. I suspect this model has “legs” to be enduring and I can imagine expansion to other settings beyond simply the ER (i.e. hospital floors, ICU, OR). This is a winner!

text:
Well, it's that time of the year: Superbowl 2025!  Our Philadelphia Eagles are playing once again against the KC Chiefs on sunday, and we are the underdogs against Mahomes et al. 
 
In this context, attached is a really interesting podcast on how the game has changed in the past 15 years, with dramatic de-emphasis of running backs in the marketplace using "money-ball" type analytics (with greater reliance on the passing game and high scores). Saquon Barkley's remarkable year or performance in the SB is unlikely to change this trend.  The memorable names like Jim Brown, Franco Harris, Walter Peyton, Eric Dickerson, Emmit Smith, et al not withstanding. 

The back story of the changes in the game, from a relative value perspective, is fascinating!  Fly Eagles Fly!
